title: The Incompetence of Incompetence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explains the Dunning-Kruger effect and its practical consequences for leaders managing underperformers. Because the skills required to do a task well are nearly the same skills needed to judge how well you're doing it, people who lack the underlying skill also lack the ability to accurately assess their own performance, leading them to overestimate their competence. The author illustrates this with weak leaders who can't recognize poor goal-setting because they don't understand what good goal-setting looks like in the first place. The recommended remedy is bringing peers and outside experts into feedback and review processes, since an under-skilled person often can't fully trust or process the leader's assessment alone. The piece closes with the sharp line that indifference to incompetence, not incompetence itself, is what ultimately damages teams.
points: The Dunning-Kruger effect: less-skilled people overestimate their competence because they lack the skill to judge it
The same skills needed to perform a task well are needed to accurately assess that performance
Involving peers and outside experts in feedback helps break the self-reinforcing loop
Change in self-assessment is typically slow but critical to future performance
quotes: The least competent people often believe they are among the most competent.
The Dunning-Kruger effect is a well-known bias that shows less skillful people tend to be largely unaware of their inadequacies.
In most cases, the skills needed to be proficient at a given task are nearly identical to those required to assess one’s competency in those same skills.
Judging your own competence depends upon your ability to think about your own skills and actions from a set of standards.

Allowing an under-skilled team member to learn how others (not just the leader) view their performance and how those peers suggest developing those critical skills can promote a learning environment conducive to overcoming the effect.
On teams, it is the indifference to incompetence that is the ultimate agony.
